text:
Draw any backend, and every arrow between two boxes is an API: one side asks, the other answers, and both must agree on how. The interview tests whether you can design that agreement to be predictable, consistent, and hard to misuse. Most answers here use one example, the page's own: a blog, with articles and their comments. Sixteen questions. Ten are worked through, and six go quickly at the end.

Question one. What makes an API restful? It models the domain as resources, each with a URL, and acts on them with the standard HTTP methods. So paths are nouns, like articles slash forty-two, never a verb like get article. Each request carries everything the server needs, with no session kept between requests. And methods and status codes mean what HTTP says they mean. Done well, a developer can guess the next endpoint. And because no request depends on the last, any server behind a load balancer can answer the next one.

Question two. Walk through the main HTTP methods and their semantics. Two properties sort them. Safe: the server's state doesn't change. Idempotent: repeating the request has the same effect as sending it once. GET reads, and is both. PUT replaces a whole resource, and DELETE removes one: both idempotent. POST submits data to be processed, like a new article, and is neither. PATCH changes part of a resource, and isn't necessarily idempotent. Two follow-ups. A second delete may answer not found, a different response, but the article is gone either way, so delete is still idempotent: the property is about state, not the reply. And a patch that sets the status to published is idempotent. One that adds one to a view count is not.
